report:
**Conclusion:** Your “no” is too absolute. Magnesium **may modestly reduce depressive symptoms**, but the evidence is limited and not strong enough to consider it an established treatment for depression.

A 2023 systematic review/meta-analysis of randomized trials found an overall benefit, but explicitly notes that individual trial findings were inconsistent. The studies are generally small, short, use different magnesium forms/doses, and include varied populations (some with magnesium deficiency or other medical conditions). Those limitations make the pooled result uncertain and do not show that magnesium treats major depressive disorder broadly.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10783196/

One often-cited 2017 trial found symptom improvement with magnesium chloride in adults with mild-to-moderate depression, but a single short trial cannot establish effectiveness, particularly compared with proven therapies.  
https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/magnesium-dosage

Low magnesium status may be associated with depression, but association does not prove that supplementing magnesium will treat it; low intake/levels can also track with illness, diet, and socioeconomic factors. The NIH’s magnesium fact sheet provides safety and interaction information but does not endorse magnesium as a depression treatment.  
https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Magnesium-HealthProfessional/

For clinically significant depression, magnesium should **not replace** evidence-based care (psychotherapy, antidepressants when indicated, and clinical follow-up). NICE’s depression guideline does not list magnesium among recommended treatments.  
https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng222

Magnesium supplements can cause diarrhea and may be risky with kidney disease or interact with some medicines. Discuss it with a clinician—especially if symptoms are severe, worsening, or include thoughts of self-harm.
